text:
Corn is normally established by direct seeding rather than by raising and transplanting seedlings, taking advantage of soil moisture available right after planting. Getting planting depth right is important for even emergence: seed placed too shallow can dry out before it germinates, while seed placed too deep -- especially in heavy or compacted soil -- can result in poor, uneven emergence because the coleoptile struggles to reach the surface.

Along with correct depth, consistent row spacing and within-row (plant-to-plant) spacing are important for establishing an even, well-distributed plant population across the field, which in turn affects both light capture and the field's ability to compete with weeds early in the season. Planting equipment ranges from simple hand dibbling to animal-drawn or tractor-mounted seeders; some seeders (as shown in the source) combine seed placement with basal fertilizer placement in a single pass, dropping fertilizer to the side of and below the seed.
